subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students
title: The Router That Ignored the Shorter-Looking Route
featured_title: THE ROUTER THAT IGNORED THE SHORTER-LOOKING ROUTE

presentation.challenge: Two routes matched the destination. The router chose the more specific prefix, not the visually simpler route.

practice.primary_question: Why does an IP router choose the longest matching prefix when multiple routing-table entries match a destination?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Choosing the route with the numerically smallest network address or shortest written prefix instead of the most specific matching prefix.

case_dna.target_misconception: If two routes match a destination, the router should use the route with the shorter prefix because it covers the network more broadly.
case_dna.why_plausible: A shorter route entry can look simpler or more general, and students may confuse 'shorter path' with 'shorter prefix.'
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For destination 10.1.2.55, both 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.2.0/24 match, but /24 contains more matching leading bits and is therefore selected.
case_dna.corrected_model: Route lookup uses the most specific matching network prefix: the longest prefix length among matching entries.

problem_statement: A router has two relevant entries: 10.0.0.0/8 via Interface A and 10.1.2.0/24 via Interface B. A packet is destined for 10.1.2.55. A technician expects the /8 route because it appears first in the table. The router sends the packet through Interface B. Diagnose the route-selection rule and identify which entry wins.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: Both routes matched. Only one was specific enough to win.
gates.prompt: What route-selection rule explains the choice?

options.label: Select the matching route with the longest prefix
options.reason: The longest matching prefix is the most specific route.

options.label: Select whichever matching route appears first in the table
options.reason: Table display order is not the IP longest-prefix-match rule.

options.label: Select the shortest prefix because it covers the largest network
options.reason: Routing lookup prefers the most specific matching prefix.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the selected prefix
gates.prompt: For destination 10.1.2.55, which prefix length wins between /8 and /24?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Run the route lookup
gates.result: The /24 route is selected because it is the longest matching prefix.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Verify the destination belongs to the /24 network
gates.prompt: For 10.1.2.0/24, how many leading bits are fixed by the network prefix?
gates.success: The /24 route fixes 24 leading bits and is more specific than the matching /8 route.
gates.hint: The number after the slash is the prefix length.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The route table contains a broad match and a specific match

cards.text: The /24 entry has more matching prefix bits, so it is chosen.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the routing note
report: C2. Both /8 and /24 entries match the destination.
C3. The router should choose the /8 route because it is broader and appears first.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: IP lookup prefers the longest matching prefix, which is /24.

evidence_choices.label: The /24 route matches 24 leading network bits versus only 8 for the /8 route
evidence_choices.reason: This directly identifies the more specific route.

correction.template: The router selects the /{prefix} route because it is the longest matching prefix.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Send only 10.1.2.x traffic through Interface B
gates.constraint: Keep the broad 10.0.0.0/8 route through Interface A.

options.label: Keep/add the specific 10.1.2.0/24 route through Interface B
options.reason: Longest-prefix match directs that subnet through B while other 10.x traffic can still use the /8 route.

options.label: Delete the /8 route entirely
options.reason: That may remove reachability for other 10.x destinations and is not required.

options.label: Add another identical 10.0.0.0/8 route through B
options.reason: That does not create a more specific destination match.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply longest-prefix match
gates.prompt: A destination matches 172.16.0.0/12 and 172.16.8.0/21. Which prefix is preferred?

options.reason: It is the longer and therefore more specific matching prefix.
It is broader, not more specific.

options.label: Either one; prefix length does not matter
options.reason: Prefix length is central to longest-prefix-match selection.

gates.explanation: Among matching routes, the longest prefix is preferred.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the route-selection rule
gates.confirmation: I confirm that IP routing chooses the most specific matching network prefix when multiple routes match.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The expected route was based on table order and breadth rather than specificity.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use longest-prefix matching among all routes that contain the destination.

seo.seo_title: Longest Prefix Match: Why /24 Beats /8 in IP Routing | FE E-040
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-040: a destination matches both /8 and /24 routes. Learn why IP routing selects the longest matching prefix.
seo.excerpt: A router can match more than one route. The winner is the most specific matching prefix, not simply the first or broadest entry.
seo.direct_answer: When multiple IP routes match a destination, a router selects the longest matching prefix. For destination 10.1.2.55, both 10.0.0.0/8 and 10.1.2.0/24 match, but /24 is more specific and is selected.

faqs.a: Choose the matching route with the greatest prefix length, meaning the most specific network.

faqs.q: Which route wins between a matching /8 and /24?
faqs.a: The /24 route, assuming no even more-specific match exists.
